title: Where Our Picture of Hell Came From
hook: Did today's fiery hell come from the Bible, or from Babylon, Greece, Rome and Dante?
tldr: The video traces today's hell through ancient underworld myths, Greek poets and Plato, Augustine, Roman emperors and the Reformers. Historians confirm much of the imagery came through Greek and Roman tradition, the Apocalypse of Peter and Dante, but they debate how far ideas were borrowed rather than developed within Judaism, and some of the video's claims are overstated.
big_idea: Much of hell's furniture came from culture; the debate is how much.

points.title: Underworlds long before the Bible
points.text: The video starts the story with Mesopotamian texts such as Gilgamesh and Inanna's descent to Ereshkigal, and with Egypt's Book of the Dead and Book of Gates, where gods vie for power over death.

points.title: Greek poets made punishment moral
points.text: In the video's account, Homer's dead are morally neutral, Hesiod's Theogony founds world order on punishing rebel gods, Aristophanes' Frogs adds moral stakes, and Virgil's Aeneid gives hell a geography.

points.title: Plato: the soul that cannot die
points.text: The video credits Plato with the undying soul and a dual nature of man. His Phaedo sends incurable souls to Tartarus forever, though curable souls are released.

points.title: Empire, Augustine and control
points.text: The video argues Constantine used Christianity to secure obedience, and Justinian made Augustine's teaching the only one, so fear of endless punishment served to keep the masses in check.

points.title: From relational to judicial theology
points.text: The video traces a chain of legally minded thinkers, Tertullian, Augustine, Luther, Calvin, then Edwards, who turned a loving Father into a retributive judge, against Zechariah 7:9's mercy and compassion.

points.title: Tours of hell and Dante
points.text: Historians add the Apocalypse of Peter (about 100-150 AD), with punishments matched to each sin, and Dante, who borrowed Charon, Minos and Cerberus from Virgil's classical underworld.

points.title: Influence, or inner development?
points.text: Some scholars see Persian and Greek borrowing; others, like Jon Levenson and Martha Himmelfarb, stress development within Judaism. Traditional Christians say Jesus himself taught hell; culture only shaped the pictures.

sections.h: Views are possibilities, shaped by upbringing
sections.summary: The video insists it believes in a biblical place or places called hell, but calls every historic view a possibility, not a certainty, since all cite Scripture. Worldview and upbringing matter: Origen, raised by loving, godly parents, found ultimate reconciliation natural; Augustine, with an absent father and his own struggles, including concubines and a child outside marriage, felt he deserved damnation. The presenter, raised a rebellious preacher's kid, once believed he deserved hell too.

The video repeats the claim that the first five centuries had six theological schools: Alexandria, Caesarea, Antioch and Edessa (or Nisibis) taught ultimate reconciliation, Carthage taught eternal punishment through Tertullian, and Ephesus taught annihilation, perhaps after an afterlife chance. This claim goes back to J.W. Hanson in 1899 and is disputed; the app's early-church and objection topics weigh it in detail.

According to the video, many scholars begin the history of an underworld with the Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh and the Sumerian tablets of Inanna, the fertility goddess who sought power over death from her sister Ereshkigal, from the early second millennium BC, with an Akkadian version too. Egypt's Book of the Dead tells of Isis, Amun-Ra, Horus and Seth contending to rule the underworld; the Book of Gates shares the theme.

The video notes Homer's Odyssey shaped the ancient world up to Socrates and Plato, yet its death is morally neutral. Hesiod's Theogony grounds divine order in punishing tyrant gods and rebels against Olympus, so divine punishment starts with the world's origin. Aristophanes' play The Frogs gave the afterlife moral stakes. Virgil's Aeneid mapped hell as a geography and was one of Augustine's favorite books; Virgil was in fact a Roman poet.

The video says Plato first claimed the soul cannot die and taught a dual nature of man, splitting sacred from secular, a worldview many early Christians brought with them. It cites Augustine praising Plato's voice as the purest and brightest in philosophy, dispelling clouds of error (Against the Academics, book 3). Plato's Phaedo keeps incurable sinners in Tartarus forever but releases curable ones, a precedent for both hell and purgatory.

The video argues Constantine made Christianity Rome's religion partly to win submission, and that telling an unlettered population that disobeying the emperor meant Hades without escape kept people in line. It says Justinian, an admirer of Augustine, defunded the other five schools and their writings were lost. Historians note Justinian's 529 decree targeted pagans, Jews and heretics, and was not aimed at those Christian schools.

The video says Augustine helped convene the Council of Carthage in 397, which recognized the canon, and would allow Revelation only if read allegorically. It traces original sin, total depravity, the sin nature and eternal torment to Augustinianism, and says he preached the gospel with fear and punishment to keep the masses in check. Over 1,500 years later these remain the predominant Western views.

The video notes Tertullian is called a lawyer, Augustine studied law, Luther studied law and Calvin was a lawyer. Together they shifted a relational theology to a judicial one: God as master and judge with retributive justice, not the mercy and compassion of Zechariah 7:9. Most scholars now doubt Tertullian was the jurist of that name, though he clearly used legal reasoning.

The video says Luther denied the blessed would grieve seeing loved ones tortured. Calvin repeated a quip that God spent the time before creation building hell for the curious, and taught double predestination. Edwards, of Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God, said hell's sight would heighten the saints' joy. Lines about hell's infants a span long are widely attributed to Calvin and Edwards but lack verified sources.

sections.h: The chain, and Milton and Dante
sections.summary: The video sums up the lineage: Edwards learned from Calvin, Calvin from Augustine, Augustine from Tertullian, and ultimately from Plato, so much of the picture was pagan. It names Milton's Paradise Lost and Dante's Inferno as later shapers. Dante drew Charon, Minos, Cerberus, the Furies and more from Virgil's underworld, systematizing torments for each sin into nine circles.

Scholars such as Mary Boyce argued Zoroastrian ideas, judgment at the Chinvat Bridge, heaven, hell and resurrection, shaped Judaism during and after the Babylonian exile. Skeptics answer that no Zoroastrian text clearly teaching resurrection predates the Jewish ones, and Jon Levenson argues resurrection developed within Israel's own faith, while granting Persia may have shaped apocalyptic thought.

sections.h: Research: Hellenization and Second Temple texts
sections.summary: Sheol in the Hebrew Bible has no fire, torment or judgment. Translated into Greek as Hades, it took on Greek associations. In 1 Enoch 22, of the third century BC, the hollow places of the dead are divided between righteous and sinners, and Daniel 12:2, often dated to the Maccabean crisis, speaks of everlasting life and contempt.

Written around 100-150 AD, this tour of hell matches each punishment to a sin, measure for measure. Martha Himmelfarb places it in a Jewish genre going back to 1 Enoch's Book of the Watchers, rejecting the older Orphic theory. Jan Bremmer grants the Jewish frame but finds clear Greek and Roman precedents, including the Orphic mud, borboros.

Historian Alan Bernstein's Formation of Hell reads Mesopotamian, Egyptian, Greek, Roman and Israelite sources and argues hell arose late in Judaism to answer worldly injustice. Traditional voices such as Ligonier reply that hell was not invented by Edwards, the Reformers, Aquinas or Augustine but comes from Jesus' own teaching; pagan sources shaped its art, not its substance.

mythfact.myth: The Bible's Sheol was always a fiery place of torment.
mythfact.fact: Sheol in the Hebrew Bible has no fire, torment or judgment; those ideas grew in Second Temple texts like 1 Enoch and with the Greek rendering Hades.

mythfact.myth: Dante's hell is simply what the Bible describes.
mythfact.fact: Dante borrowed Charon, Minos, Cerberus and others from Virgil's classical underworld and organized torments for each sin into nine circles.

mythfact.myth: Zoroastrian borrowing is a proven fact.
mythfact.fact: It is debated: Persian contact is real, but surviving Zoroastrian texts are later than the Jewish ones, and scholars like Jon Levenson argue for internal development.

mythfact.myth: Calvin wrote that hell is paved with infants a span long.
mythfact.fact: No verified source has been found for that line; Edwards' line that hell's sight will heighten the saints' happiness, by contrast, is documented.

objections.claim: Hell was not borrowed from pagans; Jesus taught it himself, so the history of other religions is irrelevant.
objections.strongest: Ligonier argues hell was not invented by Edwards, the Reformers, Aquinas or Augustine but comes from Jesus' teaching. Parallels prove nothing: Gehenna and outer darkness are Jesus' own words, and later art only decorated a biblical truth.
objections.response: This is a fair point, and the video's chain from Plato to Edwards overreaches when it calls the whole idea pagan. Jesus used Jewish words like Gehenna. But the question is how those words were heard. Sheol had no fire or torment; Greek translation turned it into Hades, Plato supplied an undying soul, and the Apocalypse of Peter and Dante supplied the vivid torments. So the debate is not whether Jesus warned of judgment but whether our picture of endless torture is his or a later Greco-Roman frame read into him.

objections.claim: The Persian influence theory is speculation; Zoroastrian texts are later than Daniel.
objections.strongest: No surviving Zoroastrian text clearly teaching resurrection or a final hell predates the Jewish writings. Similar ideas could arise independently, and Jon Levenson shows resurrection grew from Israel's own Scriptures and hopes.
objections.response: Granted, and that is why this topic leans more on documented Greek and Roman channels than on Persia. Even skeptics concede Persia may have shaped apocalyptic thought, and Second Temple texts like 1 Enoch show Jewish ideas of sorting the dead developing under foreign rule. Whether borrowed or home grown, the shift from a neutral Sheol to compartments of reward and punishment happened late, after the exile, not in the Torah.

objections.claim: The video's history of lawyers, emperors and suppressed schools is a conspiracy story, not history.
objections.strongest: Tertullian was probably not the jurist of that name, Justinian's 529 decree targeted pagans, Jews and heretics without naming any school, and the six-schools scheme comes from a nineteenth-century universalist. Blaming hell on imperial control ignores sincere believers.
objections.response: Several details should be corrected, and this topic does so. Yet the core historical point stands: Augustine's influence on Western theology, including endless punishment, was enormous, and he admitted very many in his day rejected it. Legal reasoning shaped Tertullian, Calvin and later penal frameworks, and historian Alan Bernstein shows hell took shape through prophets, priests and poets, not Scripture alone. Motives can be sincere while effects still shape doctrine.

objections.claim: Similar imagery does not prove borrowing; Christian tours of hell are a Jewish genre.
objections.strongest: Martha Himmelfarb refuted the nineteenth-century view that the Apocalypse of Peter was a Christianized Orphic descent to Hades, tracing it to 1 Enoch's Book of the Watchers. Measure-for-measure punishment is a Jewish principle.
objections.response: Himmelfarb's case for a Jewish genre is strong, but Jan Bremmer shows some of its punishments have clear Greek and Roman precedents, even Orphic vocabulary such as borboros, the mud of the underworld, and Richard Bauckham thinks Himmelfarb played down Greek debt. Either way, these vivid tortures come from writings outside the Bible that the church read and painted for centuries, which is the point the video makes about our inherited picture.

quiz.q: What does Plato's Phaedo say happens to curable souls?
options: They are purged and can be released
quiz.why: Plato kept the incurable in Tartarus forever but let curable souls out once forgiven, a precedent for both hell and purgatory.

quiz.q: Where did Dante get Charon, Minos and Cerberus?
quiz.why: Dante borrowed many figures from Virgil's Aeneid and the Greco-Roman Hades, then organized torments by sin.

quiz.q: Why do some scholars doubt Zoroastrian borrowing?
options: Surviving Zoroastrian texts are later than the Jewish ones
quiz.why: The dating problem means similarity alone cannot prove which way influence ran; Levenson argues for development within Judaism.

reflect: Which details of your own picture of hell come from Scripture, and which from art, sermons or films?
